text.p: An executive at troubled Mexican holding company Grupo Sidek said he doubted any of its creditors would seek the firm's liquidation and added it would present a financial restructuring plan in June.
Liquidation "was really just a rumor brought about by lack of more detailed information," Sidek Joint Director General Jose Franco Oyanguren told Reuters in a telephone interview late on Friday.
"What I can be sure of is that there is no move towards bankruptcy or liquidating the company for now," he added.

Sidek said on Friday that it had posted a negative majority shareholders equity as a result of its 2.43 billion peso loss for 1996. It added that under Mexican law, any interested party could request the company's liquidation through judicial proceedings in Mexico.
Sidek also said it had detected accounting and other "irregularities" by the previous management at tourism unit Situr that weakened the company's position.

Shares listed by Sidek, Situr and its steelmaking subsidiary Simec tumbled on Friday. Trading in Sidek and Simec was halted on both the New York and American Stock Exchanges. Simec early on Monday began trading again on the American Stock Exchange, while Sidek shares were still halted on Wall Street.
This morning, both Simec and Situr shares rose sharply.
The announcement, however, "does not mean that any one at the moment is seeking a process (of liquidation) for the group," Franco said.

"We cannot say no one is going to seek liquidation. There may be some small supplier that does...we are just trying to keep the public better informed of exactly what is happening to the company," he said.
A syndicate of Mexican banks that holds almost 70 percent of Sidek's debt promised in a 1996 standstill agreement not to seek liquidation until at least June 30, 1997, he said.
"By that time, we hope to be able to have offered the banks a new restructuring plan," he said, adding the company had hired Lehman Brothers as a consultant on the restructuring.
Franco would not talk about terms of the restructuring, but said it was likely it would include the sale of assets.
The company's remaining creditors, mostly bondholders in the United States and Europe, will also need to reach an agreement with the company on terms of the restructuring, he said.
Franco said the company has called for a board meeting on April 8 to present the findings of an investigation into past management irregularities, including the estimated impact on the company.
He also said he was not surprised by the 42 percent fall in the company's B shares on Friday.
"Having a negative shareholders equity was enough to cause investors to reevaluate the value of the shares according to their criteria," he said.
